facts: NBS Circular 592 (citing Kiefer and Renshaw) states that "molybdenum-bearing types 316 and 317 were the most resistant at low temperatures, but at about 150° F all of the stainless steels corrode in practically all concentrations of acid from } to 95 percent." (note: the lower concentration bound in the scanned text is OCR‑corrupted and appears as "}").
NBS Circular 592 reports Roach and Hall observed that, at room temperature, molybdenum‑bearing stainless steels were useful in sulfuric acid concentrations below 15 percent and above 85 percent.
NBS Circular 592 notes that the resistance to sulfuric acid of stainless steels is improved in some cases by additions of copper or cerium.

NBS Circular 592 describes Hastelloy A (56 Ni-22 Mo-22 Fe) as "usefully resistant to sulfuric acid of all concentrations at temperatures up to about 160° F, and up to the boiling point for concentrations below 50 percent."

Inference (screening recommendation): For service with sulfuric acid at approximately 150° F, common austenitic stainless steels (including 316/317 family) should be treated as suspect and not assumed acceptable across concentration ranges; either require specific corrosion test data for the exact alloy/concentration/temperature/aeration/flow conditions or select higher‑resistance alloys (e.g., nickel‑base Hastelloy A) — this inference is based on the NBS statements cited above.
